paragraphs.text: My name is Robby, and this is my friend Zack.
"Hi! It's nice to meet you."
Zack moved here three years ago. I still remember his first day in our classroom. A woman was with him.
"I'm Mrs. Ray," the woman said. She explained that Zack is deaf. "I'm an interpreter. My job is to help Zack learn and communicate at school."
I raised my hand. "Does Zack read lips?"
"Yes," said Mrs. Ray. "And he wears hearing aids. In the classroom he and I will use sign language to communicate."
Soon our teacher began a math lesson. I watched Mrs. Ray explaining things to Zack. They both moved their arms and hands fast. Their faces changed expression a lot.
"Wow," I thought. "Sign language is cool!"
Zack and I sat together every day in the cafeteria. Zack got really good at reading my lips. I could tell because he always laughed at my jokes!
One day Mom and I started planning my sleepover party. I looked down at the guest list.
"What's wrong, Robby?" asked Mom.
"I want to invite Zack. But it will be hard for him when everyone is talking or playing games. He'll feel left out. I wish I could talk with him more easily."
"Hmm," said Mom. "I saw a poster about a sign language class at the library. Want to go?"
"Yes!"

Mom and I went to the sign language class together. We found out there are many different kinds of sign languages. All sign languages use hand, face, and body movements to communicate words and ideas.
Mom and I learned American Sign Language. First, we learned simple words.
Hello. Good-bye. Thank you.
Then we learned the alphabet.
A, B, C.
Soon we were signing sentences!
How are you?
It's raining today.
I couldn't wait until my sleepover party. When Zack arrived, I was waiting at the door.
"Hi, Zack. Thank you for coming."
Zack grinned. "You know sign language, Robby! Awesome!"
I'm still learning sign language. But I've gotten really good at talking with my buddy Zack. Now I can laugh at his dumb jokes!
"What fish only swims at night?
"A starfish!"
I woke up in our new apartment. My bed was shaking! The ceiling fan wiggled back and forth.
Thump! My basketball rolled off a shelf. I put my pillow over my head.
Finally the shaking stopped. Mom and Dad came to my room.
"What was that?" I asked.
"It was an earthquake," said Dad. "Earthquakes occur in some parts of California. Let's make an earthquake plan tomorrow."
The next morning Dad made breakfast. Mom and I researched earthquake safety on the computer.
"If you're in bed, stay there with your head under a pillow," said Mom.
"That's what I did," I said. "But that's because I was scared!"
Mom laughed.
I read the next part. "If you're inside, you should 'drop, cover, and hold on.' What does that mean?"
"Drop to the floor and take cover under something sturdy. That way nothing will fall on you," said Mom.

"This table is a good cover," said Dad, setting down pancakes. "If there's nothing sturdy nearby, drop down next to an inside wall. Stay away from windows. Broken glass could be dangerous. And don't use the elevator!"
"Once you've found a cover, hold on to something sturdy. Put a hand over your eyes to protect them," said Mom.
"If I'm outside, should I run inside?" I asked.
"No. Move away from buildings, trees, and power lines," said Dad. "Then drop to the ground until the shaking stops."
"We'll make a disaster kit," said Mom. "Aftershocks can happen even days after an earthquake."
At the store Mom bought a flashlight, a radio, and extra batteries. I got bottled water and enough canned food to last three days. But I didn't get any peas—yuck!
Back at home, Dad put tools in our disaster kit. Mom added first aid supplies and extra clothes.
Suddenly the floor trembled!
We dropped to the floor and took cover under the table. I held a table leg and covered my eyes. I wasn't too scared this time. I knew what to do!
Hi! I'm Frank. Today I'm volunteering with my mom in San Francisco.

San Francisco is a wealthy city, but it has many homeless people. Thousands of homeless people live on the streets. They have limited access to bathrooms. Imagine that you couldn't take showers or use clean bathrooms. I'm sure you wouldn't like that. But it's a common situation for homeless people.
Doniece Sandoval is changing that. One day she heard a homeless woman crying.
"I'm so filthy." The homeless woman sobbed. "I have nowhere to take a shower."
This gave Doniece the idea for a shower bus.
What's a shower bus? Follow me! I'll give you a tour.
Mr. Jones is the bus driver. He drives the bus to different places around the city.

The shower bus used to be a normal city bus. But now it has two private bathrooms. Each bathroom has its own shower, sink, and toilet. The bus also provides towels, soap, toothbrushes, and toothpaste. And they're all free!

The shower bus changes lives. Being clean is very important, and not just for health reasons. Many homeless people can't get jobs if they aren't clean. Without jobs, they can't find housing. Being clean provides opportunities for many homeless people. In fact, the shower bus even changed my life.

My mom and I used to be homeless. We couldn't take showers or use clean bathrooms. That was before we found the shower bus. On the shower bus, we could do both! It helped my mom find a job. It also helped us find an apartment. Then we weren't homeless anymore! But we still come to the shower bus to volunteer.
That's it for our tour. Mr. Jones has to drive the bus to another part of the city. I'm glad you visited the shower bus with me. Maybe you can find a way to help the homeless too!
"Jim, here's your sleeping bag. Have fun!" Mom said.
"See you tomorrow, Mom," I said.
I was having a sleepover at Steve's house. It was my first one.
"Hi Jim!" Steve was waiting for me at the door. "Let's put your stuff in my room. Then we can go outside to rollerblade."
"Sounds great!" I said.
Steve brought me upstairs. In his room he had lots of cool toys. He also had a white guinea pig named Ghost.
Soon we were rollerblading outside.
"Watch this spin," Steve said.
"Nice move. Watch me jump," I said.
Steve's mom called us inside for dinner. "Time for pizza, boys!"
After dinner we played video games. Then we went to bed.
Steve's mom turned off the lights. "Don't stay up too late. Good night."
"Good night," we said. But we couldn't sleep. We laughed and told spooky stories until Steve's mom came back.
"Boys," she said. "It's getting late. Go to sleep, please."
"Okay," we said.
For a while we were quiet. Then— thump! Bump!
"What was that?" I whispered.
"I don't know." Steve sounded scared too.
We heard the sounds again.
"I think there's a monster in the closet!" I said.
"Oh no!" Steve pulled his blanket over his head.
I hid under my blanket too.
Thump! Bump!
Steve stayed under the covers, hiding. "I want my mommy!"
Soon it was quiet again. Slowly I peeked out.
Across the room something was moving! I was about to scream—until I realized something. "Guess what, Steve. It's not a monster. It's Ghost!"
Steve pulled the covers tighter. "A ghost?"
I burst into laughter. "Not a ghost. It's Ghost. Your guinea pig escaped from his cage!"
Steve laughed too. He got up and put Ghost back. Soon we were both asleep.
The next morning my mom picked me up. "Did you have fun?"
"Yep!" I said. "We saw a ghost!"
"What?" Mom said.
I told her about Steve's guinea pig, and she laughed.
Then we made plans for my second sleepover. Next weekend Steve was coming to my house!
Monday was Show-and-Tell Day in Brandy's class. Each week five students brought something to class. They showed it to their classmates and told them about it.
"My turn is next week," Brandy thought nervously. Last Monday Kara brought her iguana. The week before, Miyuki performed a magic trick.
"I don't have any pets or hobbies," Brandy thought. "What can I show?"
That weekend Brandy was quiet.
"Is something wrong?" Mom asked.
"What should I do for show-and-tell on Monday?" Brandy asked.
"Hmm," Mom said. "You're good at many things."
"Like what?" Brandy asked.
"Like math and . . ." Mom pointed to a shelf. "Can you please get that jar for me?"
"Sure!" Brandy was always ready to help Mom. Three years ago Mom was in a car accident. Now she used a wheelchair. Mom could do a lot for herself. But sometimes she needed Brandy's help.
Brandy handed Mom the jar.
"Thanks," Mom said. "Back to show-and-tell . . ." She reminded Brandy of some things Brandy liked to do.
Brandy did enjoy drawing and playing soccer. But nothing felt quite right for show-and-tell . . . until Sunday night!
In school the next day, Brandy felt worried. When it was time for show-and-tell, she looked nervously at the door.
"I hope this was a good idea," she thought.
"It's your turn, Brandy," Mr. Francesco said.
She looked at the door again. "I, um, maybe—"
"Hello!" The door opened. "Sorry I'm late!" Brandy's mom said.
"Phew!" Brandy thought. She joined Mom near Mr. Francesco's desk.
"I'm going to talk about my mom today," Brandy said. "As you can see, she uses a very cool wheelchair. There are lots of things she can do with it."
Brandy's mom demonstrated going forward and backward. Then she did a spin.
The class clapped.
"The wheelchair makes her life much easier," Brandy said.
"Something else makes my life easier." Mom beamed at Brandy. "My daughter helps me all the time!"
The class started clapping again. This time it was for Brandy.
"What an interesting show-and-tell!" Mr. Francesco said. "Brandy, that was a wonderful idea!"
Brandy grinned and then hugged Mom.
The rain and wind finally stopped. Sonia looked out her window. The whole neighborhood was flooded. And next door someone was trapped in the tree house!
It was her neighbor Tim. He looked scared.
"Help!" the boy yelled. "I'm trapped up here!"
The floodwater was high. Tim could not climb down the ladder.
"Stay up there," Sonia yelled to Tim. "I will call for help." She quickly found the phone and dialed 9-1-1.
"This is the 9-1-1 operator. What is your emergency?" the operator asked.
"We need help!" Sonia cried. "Our backyards are flooded. And my neighbor is trapped in his tree house!"
"What is your address?" the operator asked.
"Seven Bell Avenue in Dover," Sonia said.
"Stay calm and stay on the phone," the operator said. "What is your name? Are you safe?"
"My name is Sonia Rivera. Yes, I'm safe in my house with my parents."
"Help is on the way. Do not hang up the phone," the operator said.
Soon Sonia heard sirens. An ambulance and other emergency trucks arrived.
"Help is here," she said to the operator.
Sonia hung up the phone. Then she and her parents watched the rescue.
The rescue workers went to the tree house in a boat. They helped Tim out of the tree house. Then they took him to the ambulance.
"Thank you, Sonia!" Tim said. He didn't look scared anymore.
A rescue worker came to the front door.
"You did the right thing," he said to Sonia. "You called 9-1-1 and stayed calm. You saved Tim's life today."
Adam was going to work with Mom for the day.
"Delivering mail will be fun," said Adam. "A lot more fun than learning stuff at school."
"You're going to work hard," said Mom. "And you'll still be learning—all about helping customers."
"That sounds better than learning about fractions!" said Adam.
At the post office, Adam and Mom filled two large mailbags. Then they drove to a busy neighborhood to deliver the letters and packages.
Adam wiped sweat from his forehead. "My mailbag is so heavy. When's morning recess?"
Mom chuckled. "There's no recess when you're working!" she said. "But later we'll take a short lunch break." She pointed up a steep hill. "Follow me!"
At the top of the hill, Adam carried a package to a house.
"Woof! Woof!" A dog barked from inside.
"Shh, Peanut!" said a woman. She opened the door wider to get her mail—and the dog dashed outside.
"Oh no! My precious Peanut!" cried the woman.
Peanut charged after a garbage truck.
"I'll get him!" Adam yelled, running after the dog. They raced down the hill. Peanut chased a butterfly and a skateboarder. Finally he stopped to sniff a fire hydrant.
Adam pounced. "Gotcha!"
When Adam came back with Peanut, he was huffing and puffing.
"Good job," Mom said. "Now back to work!"
Adam groaned and followed his mother.
Their last delivery was on Chestnut Street. Adam started to put letters into the mailbox.
A man stomped angrily toward them. "My mail is late!" he growled. "I've been waiting all afternoon!"
"Very sorry, sir!" said Mom politely.
Adam and Mom drove back to the post office.
"That man was rude, Mom."
Mom shrugged. "Mail carriers have to be polite. That's a big part of the job."
At home Adam fell onto the sofa. "Phew!"
"Tired?" asked Mom.
"Yes!" said Adam. "Working was fun, but I can't wait to get back to school!"
"Rosie!" Mom called. "We're waiting!"
Rosie was juggling some tennis balls. "Coming!" she answered.
Rosie's brother Zack had a piano lesson today. After that, their brother Jimmy had a baseball game.
"Hmm," thought Rosie. "It'll be a long morning. Maybe I can practice during the boys' activities."
She put the balls in her backpack. Then she ran outside to the car.
Zack was annoyed. "What took you so long, Rosie?"
"I know what she was doing," Jimmy said. "She was practicing again."
Zack laughed. "Rosie, you can't even catch one ball! You'll never learn how to juggle!"
Rosie's cheeks turned pink. Zack was a talented piano player. Jimmy was the best hitter on his baseball team. Rosie wanted to have a talent too.
"I just have to keep practicing," she thought.
Later the family was having a snack. Suddenly they heard a boom!
"Thunder!" said Jimmy.
Outside, rain poured down and lightning flashed. Inside, the lights flickered and then went out.
Zack groaned. "We just lost our electricity."
Mom went to call the electric company.
"No TV." Jimmy sighed.
"No computer," Zack grumbled. "This is so boring."
Rosie reached into her backpack. She took a deep breath. She tossed one, two, three balls into the air.
"You're juggling!" Zack cried.
Jimmy clapped. "You did it!"
The boys watched Rosie juggle the tennis balls. Then she got some oranges and juggled those too.
"Can you teach us how to juggle?" asked Zack.
"Sure." Rosie grinned. "I finally have a talent."
Jimmy shook his head. "You have two talents."
"Two?" said Rosie.
"Yep," said Jimmy. "Juggling—and working hard!"
Annie
My brother and I had a fight today. Alex is only two years older than I am. But he always tries to boss me around!
The fight started with Mom's note.
Dear Annie and Alex,
Please clean Polly's cage. I'll be back before dinner!
We both love our parrot. Polly has pretty feathers and says funny things. But we hate cleaning her cage.
I looked at Alex. "Somebody has to clean the birdcage."
He smirked. "It looks pretty nasty. Good luck scrubbing it!"
"I cleaned it last week," I said. "It's your turn, Alex."
"Can't!" he said as he walked to the door. "I have to practice my skills. So I'm going outside to shoot some hoops. Have fun!"
"Happy Birthday!" Polly squawked.
"Ugh," I thought, looking at her dirty cage. Alex was so mean. He was so selfish too. There was no way I was cleaning the cage again!
Outside I heard his basketball bouncing on the driveway.
Suddenly I had an idea . . .
Alex
My younger sister is so annoying. She's only two years younger than I am, but she acts like a big baby.
Mom said somebody had to clean Polly's cage. I didn't mind doing it, but I do it all the time. So I asked Annie to take a turn.
Of course, Annie started whining and complaining—as usual.
"I hate cleaning the birdcage!"
"Well, it's your turn, Annie. Mom is going to be home soon, so you'd better get started."
"I'm not cleaning the birdcage!" she yelled.
"You are so!" I told her as she stormed upstairs.
"Uh-oh!" Polly squawked at me.
"Annie is such a baby," I muttered. I went outside and practiced slam dunks.
"Hmm," I thought.
"Hey, Annie. I've got an idea . . ."
Mom
When I got home, Alex and Annie were in the driveway playing basketball.
"Hi, kids. Did you clean the birdcage?" I asked.
"Yep," said Alex.
"We did it together," said Annie.
"Really?" I said. "I thought you two would argue about it!"
"We had a foul shooting contest," said Alex. "The loser was supposed to clean the cage."
"But we each scored five points," said Annie. "So—"
"You cleaned the cage together!" I said, hugging them.Polly squawked. "Good job, team!"
Drew sighed. "I have nothing to do," he said. "I'm so bored!"
He lay on the sofa and stared up at the ceiling.
Dad walked into the living room.
"What are you doing, Drew?" Dad asked.
"I'm bored," said Drew.
"Bored?" said Dad.
"There's nothing to do," said Drew. He slid off the sofa. His feet were still on the sofa. But his head was now under the coffee table.
"Hmm," said Dad. "Come with me."
Drew followed Dad to the kitchen.
"These dishes are dirty," said Dad. "Since you have nothing to do, you can wash them."
"Ugh," said Drew. He filled the sink with hot, soapy water. Then he got to work.
When Drew was done, he went back to the living room.
"Oh, hi, Drew," said Dad. "I was going to vacuum the living room. But since you're bored today, you can do it."
Drew vacuumed the living room. Next he helped Dad weed the garden. Then he peeled potatoes and set the table.
During dinner Drew was tired. "That was a busy day," he said.
Dad smiled. "Anytime you're bored, just let me know!"
Drew laughed. "I'll never say I'm bored again!"
Last year my family moved from New York City to Miami. I like my new city, but I miss my old one.
In Miami I have two new friends. Their names are Maria and Nicole. We have lots of fun together. In New York I had a best friend. Her name was Chloe. I miss Chloe a lot.

In Miami I live in a big new house. I have a bedroom all to myself. In New York I lived in a small apartment. I shared a room with my sister. Sometimes I miss sharing a room with her. We talked and laughed all night.

In Miami there is a sandy beach near my house. I often go swimming with Maria and Nicole. In New York there was a huge park near my apartment. I loved it when it snowed. I miss sledding in the park with Chloe.
In Miami it never gets cold. So I never have to wear a coat or mittens. In New York it gets very cold in the winter. I had to wear thick, warm clothes.
In New York I lived with my mom, dad, and older sister. We all moved to Miami. We still live together. We still have a wonderful family. I guess some things never change.
"You're getting a babysitter tonight," Dad said.
"I don't need one. I'm not a baby ," I complained.
"Sorry, Bobby," Mom said. "We can't leave you home alone at night."
"Fine," I grumbled. "When will Carla get here?"
"Carla has a softball game tonight," Dad said. "Mrs. Muller will babysit you instead."
"Oh no!" I thought. "She's scary!"
Mrs. Muller arrived.
"The first aid kit is in the closet," Mom said. "There's a list of emergency phone numbers on the counter. Bobby doesn't have any food allergies. And his bedtime is at ten."
Mom and Dad left.
"Did you finish your homework?" Mrs. Muller asked.
"No. Tomorrow is Saturday," I said.
"No excuses," she said sternly. "Go get started."
A little while later I went into the kitchen. "What's for dinner?" I asked.
"Turkey burgers!" she said. "And I don't want to hear any complaints!"
After dinner I asked to watch TV.
"Sure," Mrs. Muller said. "We'll watch my favorite show."
"It's probably something boring," I thought.
She flicked through the TV channels. Then she stopped at channel ten. Space Rangers was on.
I looked at her in surprise. "This is your favorite show too?"
"Of course!" she said.
After the show Mrs. Muller pointed to my video games.
"Do you have Super Ninja ?" she asked.
"Wow! You play video games?" I asked.
"I play them with my grandson," she said. "And watch out. I usually win!"
Soon it was ten o'clock.
"Time flies," she said. "It's your bedtime."
I sighed.
"Hmm," Mrs. Muller said. "I guess one more game wouldn't hurt."
"Can you be my babysitter next time?" I asked.
Mrs. Muller nodded, "Sure." She even smiled at me.
Mrs. Muller wasn't scary after all.
Kyle looked around his new room. His sleeping bag lay on the empty floor.
"I hope the moving truck comes soon," he thought.
Kyle went down to the kitchen. He opened the refrigerator and found it was empty too.
"Ugh," said Kyle.
His mom walked in with a box. Kyle heard dishes rattling inside.
"We'll go grocery shopping later," she said. "Why don’t you play outside for now? Maybe you'll make a friend."
Kyle went outside and walked down the sidewalk. He found a park. But the place was empty.
"This stinks," he thought.
"Hi," said a voice.
"Huh?" Kyle looked around, but he didn't see anybody. "Who said that?"
"I did," said the voice.
Kyle spun around. The voice was coming from a tall oak tree!
"A talking tree?" said Kyle.
"That's right," said the tree. "Want to be friends?"
Kyle scratched his head. "How can we be friends?" he asked. "I'm a person, and you're a tree!"
"Does it matter? By the way, I like cats," said the tree. "Do you?"
"Yes," said Kyle.
"I like playing soccer," said the tree. "Do you?"
Kyle couldn’t imagine a tree playing soccer. But he answered the question because he wanted to be polite.
"Yes, I love soccer," he said.
"I'm in fourth grade," said the tree. "What grade are you in?"
"I'm in fourth grade too!" said Kyle. "But how can a tree go to school?"
"Climb up and find out," said the tree.
Kyle grabbed a branch and climbed up.
A girl was chuckling on a branch.
"Hi," she said. "I'm Pearl. I like cats and soccer and . . . climbing trees."
Kyle laughed. He had a new friend!
Mike is a student at Woodlawn Elementary School. He is in the fourth grade. There are fifteen students in his class─seven girls and eight boys.

It is springtime. The students love to play outside. It's time to go to PE class. Mr. Rabinovich is the PE teacher. He is a very nice teacher. He and the students are having class outside today. It's too nice to play inside.
"What are we going to play today?" the students ask.

"Whatever you kids want to play," Mr. Rabinovich says. "It's your decision." The girls decide they want to play soccer. Seven boys decide they want to play baseball. "It's all up to Mike," Mr. Rabinovich says. "Do you want to play soccer or baseball, Mike?"
Mike, the eighth boy, looks at the other boys. Then he looks at the girls. "Well, I don't want to play baseball."
"Hooray!" the girls scream.
"And I don't want to play soccer," Mike says. Everyone is quiet.
"You don't want to play baseball, and you don't want to play soccer?" Mr. Rabinovich asks. "Well, Mike, what do you want to play?"
Mike looks at the girls. They are not happy. Then Mike looks at the boys. They are not happy either.
"Come on, Mike," one of the boys says. "Do you want to play baseball or soccer?"
"I want to play kickball," Mike says.
"You want to play kickball?" one of the girls asks.
"Yes," Mike says.
"That's stupid," one of the boys says.
"He can't choose kickball," one of the girls says. "He can only pick baseball or soccer."
The boys and girls start yelling. Everyone is angry except for Mr. Rabinovich and Mike.
"Okay, that's enough yelling," Mr. Rabinovich says. "We're going to play a game of kickball. So pick your teams."
The students pick their teams. There are three boys and four girls on one team. There are three girls and four boys on the other team. Mike is the only student not on a team.
"We don't want him on our team," the team with three boys and four girls says.
"We don't want him either," the other team says.
"Now children," says Mr. Rabinovich. "We asked Mike to choose a game to play. He chose kickball. Let him play too. But Mike, next time, remember that you can't play what you want."
So Mr. Rabinovich joins one team and Mike joins the other.
Norbert Weiner was a famous professor. He was a very intelligent man. However, he was very forgetful.
One day, the Weiner family was moving to another house. Mrs. Weiner knew that her husband wouldn't be much help moving. So she sent him to school while she and the movers worked together.

Mrs. Weiner was sure that Professor Weiner would forget that they had moved. She wrote down their new address on a piece of paper. She gave it to him and said, "Honey, this is our new address. Don't forget!"
"All right, darling," replied Professor Weiner as he kissed his wife good-bye.
"Good-bye, and have a nice day at school," said Mrs. Weiner.
While at school, Professor Weiner had a great idea. He decided to write it down in case he forgot it. He reached into his pocket and took out a piece of paper.
He wrote his idea down with a pencil. But of course, it was the piece of paper with his new address on it!
Later, Professor Weiner looked at the piece of paper again. He read his idea. He decided it wasn't very good and threw the paper away. And yes, it was the piece of paper with the new address on it!
At the end of the day, he left for home. He went to his old address. He completely forgot that his family had moved.

When he got there, the house was empty. He thought about the piece of paper from that morning. He remembered that he threw it away. But he couldn't remember the address that was written on it. He thought and thought about what to do.
The sun had set and he was very worried. Fortunately, he noticed a young girl playing behind the house.
He walked over to the girl in the darkness and said, "Excuse me, I'm Norbert Weiner and my family has just moved. Maybe you know where we've moved to?"
The young girl replied, "Yes, Daddy. Mommy knew you would forget. I'll take you home now."
Jack and his Mother are on the street in front of Jack's house.
Mother: Don't forget, Jack!
Jack: Bye, Mom!
Jack walks down the street.Lila and Mike ride by.
Jack: Two tomatoes and milk.
Lila: Hey, Jack! We're going to ride our bikes.
Mike: Do you want to go to the park?
Jack: No, I can't.
Lila and Mike: See you later!
Jack arrives at the supermarket.
Jack: Two watermelons and milk? Or two cartons of milk and some eggs?
Jack and his Mother are in the kitchen.
Mother: Thank you, Jack. What is this? Two cucumbers and . . . bread?
Jack: Sorry, Mom.
Mother: Jack . . . you forgot again!
Jack is on his way to the supermarket again. He sees a puppy.
Jack: Oh, you're so cute!
Pet store owner: Do you want to hold him?
Jack holds the puppy.
Jack returns home again.
Mother: Jack . . . I said five lemons and a can of soup.
Jack: I forgot, Mom.
Mother: What am I going to do with oranges and a bar of soap?
Jack's Mother is sick in bed.
Father: Jack, can you run to the supermarket for me?
Jack: Sure, Dad.
Father: We need some chicken soup and orange juice.
Jack tries hard not to forget.
Jack: Chicken soup and orange juice. Chicken soup and orange juice.
Mother (dreaming) : Red roses, beautiful red roses.
Father: Jack, don't forget what to buy!
Jack: Chicken soup and orange juice.
Jack walks quickly down the street.
Mike: Hey, Jack! Let's go skateboarding!
Pet store owner: Hi, Jack. Come inside and see the puppy!
Jack: No, thank you. I have to go.
Jack keeps walking.
Jack: This time, I won't forget what to buy!
Jack sees a bunch of flowers and remembers his Mother's words.
Mother: Red roses, beautiful red roses.
Jack: Oh, Mother would love these roses!
Jack returns home.
Father: Tomato soup and . . . ice cream. Jack! You forgot again!
Jack looks down. He feels bad.
Father: What are you hiding behind your back?
He shows the flowers.
Jack: I'm sorry I always forget.
Father: What are those roses for?
Mother: Roses? How did you know I wanted roses?
Jack: I heard you.
Mother: So you didn't forget the most important thing.
Mother gives Jack a shopping list.
Mother: Here is what I want you to buy, Jack.
Jack: Now I will never forget what to buy.
Jack may not remember everything. But he will never forget what is important.
Angie, Susan, Maria, and Kate went to school every morning by car. Their parents took turns driving them. One day, Susan's mother drove the girls.
After they arrived at school, Angie said, "I don't want to take the math test today. Let's go to class an hour late."
"Good idea," said Susan. "I don't want to take the test either."
"Neither do I," said Kate. "I didn't study."
"I didn't study either," said Maria. "But what are we going to tell our teacher? He will be very angry if we come late."
"Yes, we need a good excuse," said Angie.
"Oh, that's easy," said Susan. "We'll say that my mother's car had a flat tire."
All the girls agreed: it was the perfect excuse.
So, they waited for an hour. When they arrived at class, the math test was over. The teacher was very angry. "Why are you late?" he asked.
The girls all started talking at once. Finally, Susan said, "My mother's car had a flat tire. We had to wait for her to fix it."
The teacher nodded and said, "Really? Maria, sit over there in that corner. Kate, sit over there in that corner. Angie, sit here in this corner. And Susan, sit over there in that corner."
The girls did as they were told.
"Now," said the teacher, "take out a piece of paper and a pen. Each of you write down which tire Susan's mother fixed."
The girls all looked at each other!
They knew they were in trouble!
Very far away from the city lived a farmer and his wife. There was a narrow dirt road in front of their house.
On the road, there was a big hole filled with water. The hole was very deep. Drivers on the road didn't know just how deep. When they drove into the hole, they could not drive out.
One day, a man in a new car was driving down the road. He noticed the hole with the water, but he didn't think it was very deep. He drove into the hole, and his car became stuck.
The man saw the farmer on his tractor, working in the field. He waved to the farmer. The farmer drove over to the man in the new car.
"Is there a problem?" asked the farmer.
"Yes," said the man. "My car is stuck in this hole. Can you help me?"
"Maybe," said the farmer, "but I'm very busy."
"If you help me, I'll pay you," said the man.
"Okay," said the farmer.
They agreed on a price. The farmer towed the car out of the hole with his tractor. Then the man paid him the money.
The man looked at the farmer and said, "I guess you are rich. You must tow cars out of this hole day and night."
"Actually, no," said the farmer.
"Why not?" asked the man.

"The hole is very deep, and a lot of people get stuck and ask for help. But I don't make money day and night. I don't pull cars out at night. At night, I'm busy filling the hole with water," answered the farmer.
Jeffrey the Giant had many friends. Everyone liked Jeffrey because he was so kind.
When Peter’s ball got stuck in a tree, Jeffrey got it down.
"Thanks, Jeffrey," Peter said.
"Oh, you’re welcome, Peter," said Jeffrey.
When Mary hurt herself, Jeffrey carried her home.
"Oh my leg!" cried Mary.
"Are you okay? Here, let me help you up. I’ll take you home," said Jeffrey.
"Thanks, Jeffrey," said Mary.

Jeffrey liked to help his friends. But it was hard for Jeffrey to play with them. The hiding spots for hide-and-seek were too small. The jump rope was too short. The basketball hoop was too low. The seesaw always went up, but it never came down.
One day Jeffrey left the playground. He sat down under the biggest tree he could find. "I am too big to play with my friends," he said to himself. Jeffrey was sad. He lowered his head and cried.
"Hi, my name is Eddy. I’m new here. Do you want to play with me?" said a voice.
Jeffrey didn’t look up. "I’m too big to play with anyone," he cried.
"I don’t think you’re that big," said Eddy.
"Really?" asked Jeffrey.
"Yes, really," said Eddy. "You’re big like me."
Jeffrey looked up hopefully. Eddy was an elephant! "Hi," said Jeffrey surprised. "My name is Jeffrey."
Eddy smiled. "Why were you crying, Jeffrey?"
"I was crying because I am too big to play with my friends," said Jeffrey.
"You’re not too big," said Eddy. "Let’s go to the playground together and I’ll show you."
At the playground, Eddy showed Jeffrey new games to play with his friends. All the children climbed on one side of the seesaw. They all climbed on Jeffrey like a mountain.
Jeffrey and Eddy became best friends, and they had fun with the other children. But Jeffrey was glad to have such a big friend too.

20.title: It's Not Easy Being a Kid!

paragraphs.text: Hi, I'm Peter. I'm in the second grade. I have one thing to say: It's not easy being a kid! Being a kid might look like fun, but sometimes it's not.

Yesterday, I was playing outside with my friend. I was having a really good time. Then suddenly my mother said, "Peter, it's time to come inside now. It's getting dark." When you're an adult, no one can tell you what to do or when to do it.

When you're a kid, you have to get up early in the morning and go to school. At school you have to study math, English, science, and history. After school, you have to do your homework. When you're an adult, you do not have to go to school and you never have homework.

When you're a kid, there are many things you can't watch. Last Saturday there was a scary movie on TV. It looked really exciting. But my father would not let me watch. He said, "You're too young for this movie, Peter." When you're an adult, you can watch anything you want.

When you're a kid, the older kids sometimes pick on you. When I was walking home from school on Monday, Tom and Steve bothered me. Steve took my schoolbag and put it in a tree. It made me very mad. When you're an adult, no one can pick on you.

When you're a kid, you can't go anywhere by yourself. Last Friday, I wanted to buy a birthday gift for my friend John. But I had to wait for my mom to return home. When I want to go somewhere, I have to ride my bike or ask my mom for a ride. When you're an adult, you can drive a car wherever you want.
When you're a kid, you have to go to bed early. On school nights, my mom makes me go to bed at 9:00.
But I do have a mom and dad who love me, which is really great. So I guess I like being a kid, even though— it’s not easy being a kid!
It was a beautiful Sunday morning. Paula, Becky, and Helen were waiting for their mother.
"Good morning, girls!" said Dad.
"Good morning, Dad!" said the girls.
Dad began to hum as he put on Mom's pink apron.
"Where's Mom?" asked Paula.
"Your mother is sick," said Dad. "So today, I'm going to make your breakfast!"
Every Sunday, Mom made a big breakfast for the family. Mom was a wonderful cook.
The family would talk and laugh as they ate their breakfast together.
"What would you like to have?" asked Dad.
"Can I have some pancakes?" asked Becky.
"I'd like scrambled eggs and some toast," said Helen.
"May I have some bacon and sausage?" asked Paula.
"Uh . . . okay. Sure, no problem!"
"Dad, can we help?" asked Helen.
"No, thank you." Dad put the frying pan on the stove. He put two pieces of bread into the toaster.
"Now for the pancakes!"
Dad looked in the drawers, in the refrigerator, and under the sink. "Where does your mother hide the pancake mix?" Dad scratched his head.
"Mom usually keeps it in the pantry." Becky pointed.
"Dad! The frying pan!" screamed Helen.
Dad put the bacon and sausage into the smoking pan. Then he put some pancake mix into a bowl and cracked two eggs.
Ding! The toaster popped up two pieces of black toast.
"Dad, the toast . . . ," said Helen.
"Dad, the bacon . . . ," said Paula.
"Oh no!" shouted Dad.
The girls began to giggle.
"How does your mother do it? I never knew cooking was so hard! I'm sorry, girls, but I messed up our big breakfast," said Dad.
The girls ran over and hugged their dad.
"That's okay, Dad. We can have cereal!" said the girls. Paula got the milk. Becky got the cereal. Helen got the bowls and spoons.
Having a big breakfast wasn't as important as being together.
It snowed all night. The snow piled higher and higher. First, it covered the grass. Then, it covered the bushes. By morning, it even covered the cars.
"Rich and Paul! No school today!" called Mom.
"Did you hear that?" Rich asked his brother.
"Wow, no school!" shouted Paul.
Rich and Paul love snow days. They don't have to go to school. Snow days are never boring. There are so many things to do.
First, Paul and Rich make snow angels. They find a place in the snow with no footprints. Carefully, Rich and Paul lie down in the snow.
"Spread your arms and legs. Move them up and down like this," says Rich.
When they stand up, they can see angel shapes in the snow. "Ha-ha-ha!" they laugh.
Next, Paul and Rich decide to go sledding. They both have a fast sled.
"Let's race," says Rich.
"Sure! Are you ready?" says Paul. "Ready, set, go!"
They race down the hill. They go faster and faster: "Aaaaaaaah!"
"I'm the winner," says Paul. "Do you want to go one more time?"
"No, I declare war!" yells Rich.
"Wait!" shouts Paul. Rich hits Paul with a snowball.
"I'm not ready," says Paul.
Rich hits Paul with another snowball.
They have a snowball fight. Rich and Paul hit each other with many snowballs. They get covered in snow. Then Rich hits Paul with a really big snowball. It is a fun war.
"Do you want a truce?" Rich asks.
"Okay, truce. What's next?"
"How about building a snowman?"
"Sounds great!" says Paul.
Rich and Paul roll a very large snowball. Then they roll a medium-size snowball. They lift it on top for the body. The boys roll a small snowball. Then they put it on top for the snowman's head.
Rich gets coal from the garage. Paul runs into the house and gets a carrot and a hat. They give their snowman eyes, a mouth, and a nose.
Mom comes out to see the snowman.
"Look, Mom! We built a snowman. What do you think?" says Paul.
"It's great!" Mom says. "You have played for a long time. It's time to come in now."
The boys go into the house and take off their jackets and scarves. Then they sit by the fire to warm up.
"I hope it snows again tonight," says Rich.
"Another snow day would be great!" agrees Paul.
Danny woke up. He looked at the clock, turned over, and went back to sleep. The alarm woke him up again, but still he didn't get out of bed.
Danny's mother saw her son still asleep in bed. She shook him by the shoulders. "Come on, Danny. It's time to get ready for school."
"I don't want to go! I can't stand the thought of school!"
Danny's mother frowned. "Now, Danny. I know, and you know, you must go to school. I'm tired of telling you to get up every day. So, get up!"
Finally, Danny got up very slowly. He got ready for school very slowly. Danny even ate his breakfast very slowly. He chewed each piece of food for almost a minute.
Danny's mother was getting very angry. She spoke again to her son, "Look at the time! You'll be late, Danny. Finish your breakfast. You must go to school!"
Danny looked at his mother and shook his head. "I don't want to go to school. I don't care if I am late. I never want to go to school again!"
Danny's mother folded her arms across her chest. She looked sternly at her son. "Danny, you know as well as I do: you must go to school."
Danny looked up at his mother angrily. "Give me two good reasons why I should go to school."
Danny's mother rolled her eyes and then looked at her son. "First, you are 45 years old. And second, you are the principal of the school."
Danny glared at his mother. He pushed his breakfast away. He picked up his briefcase. And he slammed the door as he left for school.
In Milly Pond there lived a shy turtle called Tilly.
Tilly the turtle had no friends, because she was shy.
If anyone came by to talk or play, she would duck in her shell and wait until they went away.
Then one day Freddy the frog came swimming by.
"Tilly, don't hide in your shell. I just want to play."
But Tilly was too shy.
"No. No. Just go away."
Freddy the frog had many friends.
He knew all the fish, he liked the dragonflies, he joked with the ladybugs,
and he hung out with the bees, but his best friend was Betty the butterfly.
"Hi, Betty. How are you?"
"Hi, Freddy, I'm fine. How are you?"
"I don't think Tilly the turtle likes me.
Whenever I ask her to come out and play, she hides in her shell and won't come out until I go away."
"Oh, Freddy. I think Tilly likes you, but she is very shy."
"I don't understand. Why is Tilly the turtle shy?"
"I don't know, but I have a story."
"Oh, I like stories."
"Well, many caterpillars are shy because caterpillars think they are ugly.
I have known many caterpillars who wrap themselves up all winter, and hide away."
"When it's cold, I hide away too."
"Yes, but caterpillars are very lonely all winter, and their loneliness changes them."
"Oh, I see. When I hide away, I'm with my family. It's hard to be lonely in my family."
"In the spring, the caterpillars come out, but they are no longer ugly caterpillars who are shy; they are instead, beautiful butterflies."
"So, should I wait for Tilly to turn into a butterfly?"
"No, you should keep asking her to come out and play because one day she'll come out of her shell, just like a butterfly comes out of a cocoon."
Freddy liked Betty best because Betty was smart, and Freddy kept asking Tilly to come out and play.
One day when he was just swimming by, he said to Tilly,
"You can't have any friends if you hide in your shell. I think you should come on out and give it a try."

Tilly was lonely and she knew that Freddy was right. She had no friends because she always hid in her shell. So, Tilly poked her head out and looked all around, and she was amazed at how many new friends she found.
If you are shy and lonely, then learn a lesson from Tilly the turtle.
To find a friend, you need to come out of your shell.
"Happy needs to go for a walk," says Mother. "Take him for a walk around the neighborhood. Here's a basket and a shopping list. Please get everything on the list for dinner."
So now, Happy and I are walking down the street.
Happy is wagging his tail. He loves going for a walk around the neighborhood. All the store owners know us. And Happy loves all the strange and wonderful smells.
First, I go into the bakery. Mrs. Thompson always gives me a cookie with lots of chocolate chips. I buy some garlic bread.
"Bye, Mrs. Thompson. Thank you!" I say.
There's Mr. James, the butcher. He's always singing Italian songs. He wears a white apron. He sells all kinds of meat: pork, beef, and chicken. He throws Happy a bone. Happy loves the butcher shop!
My favorite store is Purdy's Chocolate House. The girl who works there goes to my school. She is in grade seven. Her mom makes the best fudge. Sometimes she lets me lick the spoon.
We have two more things to get for Mommy: fish and cucumbers.
Happy and I go to the fish market down by the river. The men at the fish market call out to the customers, "Salmon! Two big ones!"
"Hi, Jimmy, how's Happy?" the man asks.
At the vegetable market, the cucumbers are in a basket. Mrs. Sanderson wipes off two cucumbers with a towel. Then she puts them in a brown paper bag. She also gives me an orange.
"Here you go, Jimmy!" she says.
When we get home, Mommy is very pleased with our shopping.
"Did the people in our neighborhood help you?" she asks.
"Yes, they did," I say. "I got a cookie and an orange. And Happy got a bone!"

Wendy was a happy girl, but she didn't have a hobby. All her friends had hobbies, but she didn't have one. Her friend Julie liked to play the violin. Her friend Michelle liked to collect dolls. But Wendy didn't play any instruments and her room wasn't big enough to collect anything.
One day Wendy was with her grandma. She asked her grandma. "Grandma, what's your hobby?"

Wendy's grandma smiled a great big smile. "You know, for many years, I didn't think I had a hobby. All my friends had hobbies, but I didn't have one. One of my friends liked to play the piano. One of my friends liked to collect postcards. But I didn't play any instruments and I didn't have a room big enough to collect anything.

"But then, one day, I asked my grandmother what she collected. And she told me she was a dream collector. Dreams don't take up any space, so you will always have enough room. Dreams don't require any special skills. Dreams can't be stolen. And dreams can last forever. My grandma had many dreams in her collection."
Wendy thought for a moment. She was a good dreamer. She already had many dreams in her collection. And then she understood; she had always been a dream collector.
She looked at her grandma and smiled. "Grandma, I'm a dream collector, too."
